Two equal trains, each with 31 numbered wagons, travel in opposite directions. When the wagon number 7 of a train is side by side with the wagon number 12 of the other train, which wagon is side by side with the wagon number 11 ?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram has two rows of trains, upper and lower, with opposite directions. The locomotive of the upper train is on the left, the arrow points left, and the carriage numbers start behind the locomotive and go to the right in order as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...; the locomotive of the lower train is on the right, and the arrow points right, so its carriages in the diagram from right to left are in order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5..., that is, viewed from left to right the numbering order is reversed. Reasoning: Since the carriage lengths of the two trains are equal, and the numbers in the horizontal direction increase for one and decrease for the other, the sum of the two carriage numbers side by side at the same moment remains constant. The problem gives that carriage 7 of one train is side by side with carriage 12 of the other train, so this constant sum is 7 + 12 = 19. If carriage 11 is side by side with carriage x of the other train, then 11 + x = 19, so x = 8.

method.method_draft: Use the diagram to establish the ordering convention: on the upper train, wagon numbers increase away from its engine in one horizontal direction, while on the lower train, because the train faces the opposite way, the numbered wagons appear in the reverse horizontal order. From the text, take the given alignment: wagon 7 on one train is beside wagon 12 on the other. For equal wagon lengths, aligned wagon pairs along the two opposite-facing trains have a constant sum of indices. Thus 7 + 12 = 19. If wagon 11 on the first train is aligned with wagon x on the other, then 11 + x = 19, so x = 8.
